Block sort, or block merge sort, is a [sorting algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorting_algorithm) combining at least two [merge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merge_algorithm) operations with an [insertion sort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insertion_sort) to arrive at O(n log n) (see [Big O notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation)) [in-place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-place) [stable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorting_algorithm#Stability) sorting time. It gets its name from the observation that merging two sorted lists, A and B, is equivalent to breaking A into evenly sized blocks, inserting each A block into B under special rules, and merging AB pairs.

One practical algorithm for O(n log n) in-place merging was proposed by Pok-Son Kim and Arne Kutzner in 2008.[[1]](#cite_note-kim2008-1)

The outer loop of block sort is identical to a [bottom-up merge sort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merge_sort#Bottom-up_implementation), where each level of the sort merges pairs of subarrays, A and B, in sizes of 1, then 2, then 4, 8, 16, and so on, until both subarrays combined are the array itself.

Rather than merging A and B directly as with traditional methods, a block-based merge algorithm divides A into discrete blocks of size √A (resulting in √A number of blocks as well),[[2]](#cite_note-mannilla-2) inserts each A block into B such that the first value of each A block is less than or equal (≤) to the B value immediately after it, then locally merges each A block with any B values between it and the next A block.

As merges still require a separate buffer large enough to hold the A block to be merged, two areas within the array are reserved for this purpose (known as internal buffers).[[3]](#cite_note-kronrod-3) The first two A blocks are thus modified to contain the first instance of each value within A, with the original contents of those blocks shifted over if necessary. The remaining A blocks are then inserted into B and merged using one of the two buffers as swap space. This process causes the values in that buffer to be rearranged.

content.text:
**Block sort** (a.k.a. block merge sort).

It's the sort that ticks every box: stable, in-place (O(1) auxiliary space), worst-case O(n log n), and best-case O(n) — confirmed against Wikipedia's infobox. It works by combining bottom-up merge passes with insertion sort, using two "internal buffers" carved out of the array itself so no extra memory is needed.

Near-misses for context: Timsort matches the complexities and stability but needs O(n) extra space, and insertion sort is stable/in-place with O(n) best case but O(n²) worst case.
